title: Binary Search in under 3 minutes: win the number game every time
summary: Binary search explained with a simple number-guessing game, a step-by-step visual of low, mid and high, and the two classic Python mistakes.
author: Vinay Mishra
original_value: Teaches binary search through a ten-guess number game, then shows low, mid and high moving across an array one step at a time, and ends on the two mistakes beginners really make in Python.
sources: The standard binary search algorithm, as taught in any algorithms textbook
Python language reference: integer division (//) versus true division (/)

scenes.headline: 1 to 1000. Ten guesses.
scenes.narration: I am thinking of a number between one and one thousand. You get ten guesses, and I will only say higher or lower. Can you win every single time? Yes. And the trick is a tiny algorithm called binary search.

scenes.chapter: The slow way and the smart way
scenes.headline: Which player are you?
scenes.narration: Most people guess one, then two, then three. That is linear search, and the worst case is a thousand guesses. The smart player guesses five hundred. Higher or lower, half of the numbers are gone in one move.

scenes.headline: Binary search
items: Too big? Drop the right half
Too small? Drop the left half
scenes.narration: Here is the entire idea. Start with a sorted list. Look at the middle. If the middle is too big, throw away the right half. If it is too small, throw away the left half. Repeat until you find it.

scenes.headline: Low, mid, high

steps.note: 16 is smaller than 23, so go right
56 is bigger than 23, so go left

scenes.narration: Let us find twenty three. The middle is sixteen. Too small, so everything on the left is gone. The new middle is fifty six. Too big, so the right side is gone. Now the middle is twenty three. Found, in three looks instead of six.

scenes.headline: Eight lines
scenes.narration: In code, low and high mark what is still possible. Compute the middle. If it matches, return it. If it is too small, move low past the middle. Otherwise move high below it. If they cross, the number is not there, so return minus one.

scenes.headline: Where beginners slip

right.title: Fix
items: Sort first, or just loop through it
Use // so mid is a whole number

scenes.narration: Two classic mistakes. First, binary search only works on a sorted list. On a messy list it gives wrong answers. Second, in Python a single slash makes a decimal, and a list index cannot be a decimal. Use the double slash.

scenes.headline: A million numbers?
scenes.narration: Pause and think. If a list has one million numbers, about how many guesses does binary search need in the worst case?

scenes.headline: Halving, again and again
scenes.narration: About twenty. Every guess halves what is left. A thousand becomes five hundred, then two fifty, and about ten guesses later, one. Written in big O notation, that is log n. A million items cost only about twenty guesses.

scenes.headline: Four lines to keep
scenes.narration: To remember it: a sorted list only, check the middle, throw away half, and the cost is about log n guesses. Next time, we use it to solve a real interview problem.
